rows.answer: Mutual funds may avail intraday borrowings for all unitholder pay‑outs such as redemptions, IDCW pay‑outs, interest etc. [1] They may also use intraday borrowings for pay‑in with respect to investments made by the scheme. [1] Borrowings can be used to meet mark‑to‑market obligations and foreign exchange settlements. [2] Finally, intraday borrowings may be used for repayment of existing borrowings. [2]
The intraday borrowing conditions apply from September 1, 2026.[1]
The cost of intraday borrowing, if any, is borne by the AMC (Asset Management Company). [1]

No, a mutual fund may not borrow more than twenty per cent of the net assets of a scheme; any borrowing must be limited to that threshold unless it is intraday borrowing, for which the twenty‑per‑cent limit does not apply subject to conditions specified by the board [1].

The risk‑ometer displays six risk levels: Low risk (Irish Green), Low to Moderate risk (Chartreuse), Moderate risk (Neon Yellow), Moderately High risk (Caramel), High risk (Dark Orange), and Very High risk (Red) [1].
A Large Cap Fund must invest at least 80% of its total assets in large‑cap stocks[1].
The open‑ended scheme must have at least 20 investors, and no single investor may hold more than 25% of the scheme’s corpus.[1]
The certification examination for mutual fund distributors is conducted by the National Institute of Securities Markets (NISM) [1]. This requirement is effective from 1 April 2026 [1].

The Master Circular for Mutual Funds issued on 20 March 2026 (HO/24/13/11(1)2026‑IMD‑POD‑1/I/7602/2026) is the one currently in force, having come into effect on 1 April 2026 and replacing the earlier circular dated 27 June 2024.[1]
The Master Circular for Mutual Funds that was in force in January 2021 is SEBI/HO/IMD/DF2/CIR/P/2020/156, issued on 24 August 2020 and effective from that date【1】.

The regulations permit a mutual fund to borrow only to meet temporary liquidity needs and cap such borrowing at no more than 20 % of the scheme’s net assets, with the borrowing period limited to a maximum of six months.[1]
80% of total assets must be invested in large cap stocks [1].

The July 10 2026 circular superseded the earlier guidelines on borrowings of mutual funds – specifically clause 5.9.1 of the SEBI Master Circular for Mutual Funds dated 20 March 2026 and SEBI Circular HO/(92)2026-IMD-POD-2/I/7885/2026 dated 25 March 2026[1].
The July 3 2026 Gazette Notification CG‑MH‑E‑07072026‑274229 amended the SEBI (Mutual Funds) Regulations, 2026 to allow mutual funds to undertake intraday borrowings for various purposes.
The SEBI (Mutual Funds) Regulations, 2026 replaced the SEBI (Mutual Funds) Regulations, 1996.[1]
It replaced the Master Circular for Mutual Funds dated June 27, 2024.[1]
